title: Analyst Briefing Deck (Draft v1) — Redwood Inference: Latency per Dollar Benchmark Report
content:
Working draft deck for analyst briefings. Format: slide titles + bullets + speaker notes. This is V1 for dry-run; expect edits after claims/methodology review.

====================
Slide 1 — Title
====================
Title: Redwood Inference — Production Economics Benchmarks (Latency per Dollar)
Subtitle: Reproducible benchmark methodology + findings across model families and cloud regions
Presenter(s): Camila Reyes (Marketing), Jonas Weber (Applied ML)
Date: [TBD]

Speaker notes:
- Goal for this briefing: share the “why” (production economics), “how” (methodology/controls), and “what we learned” (headline findings + practical implications). 
- Keep this grounded: we’ll discuss variance, constraints, and what’s not measured.

====================
Slide 2 — Agenda
====================
- Market framing: from model selection to serving economics
- Redwood Inference overview (30 seconds)
- Benchmark overview: what we measured + why
- Methodology & credibility: controls, variance, QA
- Headline findings: patterns by model family + region
- How customers use it: buying decisions + engineering decisions
- Roadmap / refresh cadence
- Q&A (including hard questions)

Speaker notes:
- We’ll avoid “we’re best” claims; focus on repeatable measurement and decision usefulness.

====================
Slide 3 — The shift: Model capability is table stakes; serving is the differentiator
====================
- Open models are improving quickly; adoption is widening
- Teams now compete on:
  - Latency and tail latency under load
  - Unit cost per useful token
  - Reliability and graceful degradation
  - Deployment flexibility (hosted, dedicated, private)
- Result: procurement and engineering need a shared, defensible metric for “performance per dollar”

Speaker notes:
- Analysts see the same pattern across infra categories: differentiation moves down the stack to operational excellence and economics.

====================
Slide 4 — Why “latency per dollar” (and not just $/token)
====================
- $/token alone misses the user experience dimension
- Latency alone misses the economic reality (especially under concurrency)
- Latency/$ is designed to capture production tradeoffs:
  - How much latency you can buy for a given spend
  - Comparable across regions when controlled (same workload + same harness)
- We still report the components (p50/p95 latency, throughput, cost per 1M tokens)

Speaker notes:
- We will define latency/$ explicitly in the methodology slides. 
- Important: we do not claim it is the only metric; it is one lens.

====================
Slide 5 — Redwood Inference (one slide overview)
====================
- Developer-first platform to run and optimize LLM inference across:
  - Hosted API
  - Dedicated capacity
  - Private deployments (VPC / on-prem)
- Core: high-throughput serving runtime + orchestration + observability
- Built for production economics: batching, caching, smart routing, rollouts, fallbacks

Speaker notes:
- Keep this short. Analysts mostly care about whether the benchmark is a marketing stunt or anchored in real product differentiation.

====================
Slide 6 — What this benchmark report is (and is not)
====================
What it is:
- A public-facing, reproducible benchmark report focused on production economics
- Reported per region, across a curated set of high-demand open models
- Designed for engineering + procurement: actionable tables, not just hero charts

What it is not:
- Not customer traffic replay (no customer data)
- Not a claim of universal superiority (results include variance + constraints)
- Not a single “winner” leaderboard (emphasis on patterns and tradeoffs)

Speaker notes:
- We explicitly avoid publishing raw per-request logs or traces.

====================
Slide 7 — Coverage: workloads, models, and regions (high level)
====================
Workloads included:
- Chat generation baseline (streaming enabled)
- Embeddings baseline

Coverage design principles:
- Representative concurrency + input/output length distributions
- Consistent harness + measurement windows across regions
- Repeat runs + rerun policies when variance exceeds thresholds

Regions:
- North America + Europe baseline
- At least one APAC region (for global comparability)

Speaker notes:
- Keep model list generic in the deck unless we have final sign-off (avoid name-specific claims in pre-briefing versions).

====================
Slide 8 — Methodology: how requests are generated
====================
- Prompt sets / input distributions:
  - Chat: mix of short + medium contexts, with a realistic tail
  - Output lengths: mixture to reflect typical product UX (short answers + longer completions)
  - Embeddings: fixed batch shapes to reflect common indexing + query patterns
- Concurrency:
  - Tested at multiple concurrency levels; report uses normalized view (include appendix)
- Warmup:
  - Explicit warmup phase; results exclude warmup window

Speaker notes:
- Analysts will ask: “Is this synthetic?” Answer: yes (for reproducibility), but shaped to represent real production distributions.

====================
Slide 9 — Methodology: measurement, variance, and rerun policy
====================
We measure:
- Latency distribution (p50 / p95) and throughput
- Cost attribution per 1M tokens (or per unit for embeddings)
- Derived metric: latency per dollar (defined next slide)

Controls:
- Fixed harness + config per run
- Region-level capacity windows with safety limits
- Rerun triggers when variance exceeds thresholds
- Infra noise triage process (suspected noisy neighbors, transient region events)

Speaker notes:
- Mention that the harness includes variance summaries and automated rerun triggers (internal tooling maturity signal).

====================
Slide 10 — Definition: Latency per dollar (what exactly is computed)
====================
- We compute:
  - p50 latency and p95 latency for each run
  - cost per 1M generated tokens (and/or blended, depending on workload)
- Latency/$ is derived from latency and cost using a standardized unit definition:
  - “Latency per $” = latency metric divided by cost metric, with consistent scaling
- We report both p50-based and p95-based views (p95 emphasized for production SLO discussions)

Speaker notes:
- Avoid getting lost in units during the live briefing; point to methodology appendix in the published report.
- If asked: “Is it latency divided by $/token?” clarify the exact formulation used in the harness, and that we always provide the underlying components.

====================
Slide 11 — Credibility: QA, review gates, and claim discipline
====================
Credibility work:
- Separate owners for execution (Perf/Evals) and messaging (Marketing)
- QA sign-off checklist for outliers + anomaly triage
- Review gates for external claims (language, disclaimers, confidence/variance)
- Guardrails so benchmark runs do not impact production SLOs

Speaker notes:
- Analysts respond well to “process maturity”: independent sign-off, documented playbooks, reproducibility focus.

====================
Slide 12 — Headline findings (patterns, not winners)
====================
(Insert 2–3 headline bullets once final numbers are locked)
- Pattern A: latency/$ varies meaningfully by region even for the same model family
- Pattern B: differences are often driven by tail latency under concurrency, not just p50
- Pattern C: throughput and batching efficiency create step-changes in cost effectiveness

Speaker notes:
- In V1: placeholders only; do not commit to specific deltas.
- Avoid “X% better” until final confidence language is approved.

====================
Slide 13 — Finding: Region-to-region variance is real and operationally relevant
====================
- Same model + same harness can behave differently across regions due to:
  - Fleet heterogeneity
  - Network + upstream dependencies
  - Capacity pressure and autoscaling behavior
- Practical takeaway:
  - Buyers should ask for per-region data
  - Operators should use routing + fallback policies to keep SLOs

Speaker notes:
- Tie to Redwood’s “smart routing + fallbacks” differentiation without saying “our region is always best.”

====================
Slide 14 — Finding: Tail latency dominates perceived quality at scale
====================
- p95 is often the binding constraint for production UX
- Under concurrency, small architectural/runtime differences can have outsized tail impact
- Practical takeaway:
  - Benchmarking should include concurrency, not just single-request tests

Speaker notes:
- Analysts will compare to common public benchmarks that run at low concurrency.

====================
Slide 15 — How customers use the report (two decision paths)
====================
Engineering path:
- Choose model family + region
- Set SLOs and understand tail behavior
- Tune batching/caching + routing policies

Procurement path:
- Compare deployment options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
- Build a cost/latency envelope with documented assumptions
- Ask vendors about variance, guardrails, and reproducibility

Speaker notes:
- Point: this is meant as a “buyer’s tool,” not only a Redwood marketing asset.

====================
Slide 16 — Competitive framing (careful / claim-safe)
====================
- Market reality: many providers show single-number claims without disclosing workload + concurrency
- Our stance:
  - Publish methodology
  - Provide per-region tables
  - Report variance and constraints
- Differentiation emphasis:
  - Production economics tooling (observability, rollout controls, fallback policies)

Speaker notes:
- Keep competitor names out unless analysts ask directly. If asked, answer using methodology and what’s comparable vs not comparable.

====================
Slide 17 — Launch plan (what becomes public)
====================
Public deliverables:
- Landing page + downloadable PDF report
- Methodology appendix and FAQ
- Public data tables (sanitized subset)

Internal enablement:
- Sales field deck + objection handling
- Support readiness macros + escalation path

Speaker notes:
- Mention we’re aligning messaging across Marketing/Sales/Support to prevent confusion during inbound.

====================
Slide 18 — Roadmap: where we go next (analyst-relevant)
====================
Benchmark program roadmap:
- Expand model coverage (based on demand + strategic families)
- Expand region coverage (more APAC + additional EU options)
- Add workloads:
  - Tool/function calling patterns
  - RAG-ish retrieval + generation mix (where reproducible)
- Refresh cadence:
  - Planned periodic updates with versioned tables

Product roadmap tie-ins (high level):
- Deeper “Optimize” recommendations driven by observed bottlenecks
- Better routing/fallback policies surfaced in Console
- Continued work on Private deployments (regulated workloads)

Speaker notes:
- Keep roadmap non-committal in dates; focus on direction.

====================
Slide 19 — What we want from analysts
====================
- Feedback on:
  - Metric framing (latency/$) and what else analysts expect buyers to ask for
  - Readability of methodology appendix
  - How to communicate variance without undermining usefulness
- Collaboration:
  - Briefings during/after launch week
  - Optional follow-up deep dive with Perf/Evals team

Speaker notes:
- Ask directly: “What would make this benchmark credible to you?”

====================
Slide 20 — Q&A
====================
- Open Q&A
- If time: appendix deep dive


============================================================
APPENDIX (for hard questions)
============================================================

Appendix A1 — Hard question: “Is this cherry-picked?”
- We publish the methodology and the workload distributions
- We run consistent harness/config across regions
- We include variance reporting and rerun rules
- We do not selectively omit outliers without documented triage

Appendix A2 — Hard question: “How do you attribute cost?”
- Cost per 1M tokens derived from metering aligned to serving configuration
- We report both throughput and cost so it’s explainable
- If asked: we can share high-level assumptions used for public tables (without exposing sensitive infra costs)

Appendix A3 — Hard question: “Is caching/batching ‘unfair’?”
- Production reality uses caching and batching; excluding them can be less representative
- We document policies explicitly (warmup, cache behavior)
- We avoid hidden tuning per-model; configs are standardized

Appendix A4 — Hard question: “Do you compare against vendor X?”
- In the public report, we focus on Redwood-run measurements under documented conditions
- For external comparisons, we only compare where methodology and constraints are equivalent
- We won’t present apples-to-oranges deltas as conclusions

Appendix A5 — Hard question: “What about quality (accuracy)?”
- This benchmark is about serving economics; we do not claim quality superiority
- We encourage users to pair economics data with their own evals
- Roadmap: integrate quality regression checks tied to prompt sets

Appendix A6 — Hard question: “Can customers reproduce this?”
- We provide a minimal reproduction guide / example harness
- Customers can run a smaller-scale version against their workloads and compare patterns
